premises.text: Mass outlets cannot stock niche colors because volume-discount supply chains force them to carry only mass-selling shades, while prestige color selection is expensive
premises.evidence_span: Walmart can't offer you all the colors that expensive prestige stores can, like Sephora. Why? Supply chain

premises.text: A desktop inkjet-like printer can turn any digital image or hex color into wearable FDA-compliant makeup at home
premises.evidence_span: Mink is a desktop printer that prints makeup. It can take any image and instantly transform it into a wearable color cosmetic

premises.text: No new software is required—ordinary color pickers and print software plus commodity ink and substrates from trusted-brand sources suffice
premises.evidence_span: You do not need any new software. All you need is a color picker to copy the hex code and any software to print

premises.text: Hardware at about $300 with commodity-priced ink and substrates keeps the offering accessible
premises.evidence_span: I'm going to retail this for about $300 initially. And the ink and the substrates are going to be commodity priced

premises.text: Girls ages 13 to 21 who already learn makeup online are the beachhead customers who will grow up with the product
premises.evidence_span: My initial target market, they're girls, ages 13 to 21. They have not formed any habits yet

domains.name: Mass vs prestige color access gap

value.text: Internet-wide color selection with home convenience for makeup buyers
value.evidence_span: It gives you the selection of prestige and it combines it with the convenience of mass

secondary_value.text: Girls learn that beauty is something they control rather than corporations
secondary_value.evidence_span: The definition of beauty is something that they should be able to control, not our corporations

causal_links.evidence_span: if you want like the cool niche colors, you have to go to expensive Sephora
turning any phone, laptop, or camera into an endless beauty aisle
clicking to print is just the next natural step

notes: Future print categories (lipsticks, powders, creams) and developer sign-up folded into the printer platform rather than split (v1.3.2 clarification 5). Inventor/HBS biography excluded per 4.2. Industry size figures treated as framing. Price and consumables kept one commercial premise with beachhead in D3. Singleton D1 retained: retail color-assortment failure is independently revisable. Anti-template note: domains are market gap, printer mechanism, and pricing/beachhead—not a desirability/feasibility/viability label triad.
